transcript.text: The sides of our new fridge freezer get really warm, almost hot, especially near the front edge. Is that a fire risk? It's in an alcove between two units.

## Warm sides are almost certainly normal

Many modern fridge freezers have the condenser built into the side panels rather than as the black grille on the back. The condenser is where the fridge dumps the heat it removes from inside, so the sides are designed to get warm. They can feel quite hot to the touch, typically around 30–45°C.

The extra warmth near the front edge is also expected. Most models run a warm pipe around the door opening (sometimes called an anti-condensation or "hot gas" loop). It stops moisture forming and freezing where the door seal meets the cabinet, so that area is often the warmest part.

New fridges can also run warmer than usual for the first day or two while they pull down to temperature, and in warm weather.

## The alcove matters

Because the sides are shedding heat, a fridge with skin condensers needs room to breathe. If it's squeezed tightly between units:

• It works harder, uses more electricity, and may wear out sooner
• The sides can get hotter than intended
• It may struggle to keep cold

Check the installation section of the manual (or search the model number online) for the required side, back, and top clearances. Often it's around 5–10 cm at the sides and a gap at the top, but it varies a lot by model. Some fridges are designed to sit flush and vent elsewhere; others aren't. If yours needs more space than it has, that's worth fixing, mostly for efficiency and lifespan.

## When it would be a concern

Contact the manufacturer or retailer (it should be under warranty), and unplug it if there's any sign of burning, if you notice:

• A burning, melting plastic, or electrical smell
• Discoloration, scorching, or soft or warped plastic on the fridge or adjacent units
• Sides so hot you can't keep your hand on them for a few seconds
• The plug, socket, or cable feeling warm (this is the real fire-risk sign, unlike warm side panels)
• Crackling, sparking, or the fridge running nonstop without getting cold

## Quick safety tips

• Plug it directly into a wall socket, not an extension lead or adapter
• Make sure the cable isn't crushed behind the fridge
• Register the appliance (in the UK, at registermyappliance.org.uk) so you'll be notified of any recalls

If none of the warning signs apply, what you're feeling is the fridge working as designed. Just make sure it has the clearance the manual asks for.

Thanks, that's reassuring. There's no burning smell and no scorching or tripping, and the plug isn't warm. I can keep my hand on the sides, like a radiator on low. The gap is only about 1cm each side, with a few cm above. Is that enough?

## Probably not, but check the manual

What you describe (warm like a radiator on low, no smell, plug cool) sounds like normal operation, so this isn't a fire-safety issue. The question is efficiency and lifespan.

For a freestanding fridge freezer with condensers in the sides, 1 cm is tight. Many manufacturers ask for more, sometimes 5 cm or more per side, and some ask for 10 cm or more above. A few models are designed for close fitting and need very little side gap. The only way to know is the installation clearances in the manual or on the manufacturer's website (search the model number plus "installation" or "clearance").

## If it needs more space

• Can you gain a few cm? Pull it forward slightly so the sides aren't fully boxed in, or shift it to one side to give one side a proper gap. Even improving the airflow at the top helps, since warm air rises and escapes there.
• Keep the top gap clear. Don't store boxes, trays, or bottles on top or in the space above.
• Leave a gap at the back too (often a few cm), and don't push it right against the wall.
• If it simply won't fit properly, you may be within the return window. It's worth asking the retailer whether a model designed for tighter alcoves would suit better.

## Signs the tight fit is causing problems

• It runs almost constantly
• It struggles to stay cold (fridge around 3–5°C and freezer around −18°C are good targets)
• The sides get noticeably hotter over time, especially in warm weather
• Higher electricity bills than expected

## Quick safety tips (finishing my earlier list)

• Plug it directly into a wall socket, not an extension lead or adaptor.
• Make sure the cable isn't crushed or kinked behind the fridge.
• Vacuum dust from any vents or the back grille once or twice a year.
• Register the appliance with the manufacturer so you'll hear about any safety recalls.

You're fine from a fire point of view. The main gain from more space is a fridge that works less hard and lasts longer.
